## Industry Problem

<!--
  instructor: Ask "who owns the code for the system that would answer this?"
  before revealing it isn't the agent team. Land the distinction from 1_2's
  custom tools: you don't own or want to maintain the network-status service,
  you just want to borrow its tools. That's the whole reason MCP exists.
-->

A customer asks a telecom support agent: *"Why is my internet down?"* The real answer lives in a network-status system your team doesn't own the code for — a different team maintains it, in a different language, on a different release cycle. You can't just import their Python function.

## Instructor Example / Demonstration

<!--
  instructor: Live-run this as two files (server + client) side by side, not
  one notebook cell — students need to see that the MCP server is a wholly
  separate process the agent talks to, not code they wrote. Prereq: pip
  install langchain-mcp-adapters + fastmcp. If a live subprocess is too
  fiddly for the room, fall back to the hosted example
  (https://docs.langchain.com/mcp) which needs no local server at all.
-->

Here's the fix: stand up an MCP server exposing the lookup as a tool, and let any agent connect to it — no custom integration code required on the agent side.

```python
# network_server.py — a small MCP server, owned by the network team
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Network")

@mcp.tool()
def check_outage(zip_code: str) -> str:
    """Check whether there is a known network outage in a ZIP code."""
    known_outages = {"84604": "Outage reported, ETA 2 hours", "84601": "No known outages"}
    return known_outages.get(zip_code, "No data for that ZIP code")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")
```

```python
# agent.py — the support agent, owned by your team
import asyncio
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient
from langchain.agents import create_agent

async def main():
    client = MultiServerMCPClient({
        "network": {
            "transport": "stdio",
            "command": "python",
            "args": ["/path/to/network_server.py"],
        }
    })
    tools = await client.get_tools()
    agent = create_agent("google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash", tools)
    response = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is there an outage near 84604?"}]}
    )
    print(response["messages"][-1].content)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

Notice `agent.py` never imports anything from `network_server.py` — `client.get_tools()` is the entire integration.

## Run It Yourself

<!--
  instructor: ~10 min. Most common snag: relative vs. absolute path in `args`
  — the docs explicitly call for an absolute path to the server file, and a
  relative one fails silently-ish (connection error, not an obvious message).
  Have them print `tools` right after `get_tools()` so they see the schema
  MCP generated before the agent ever runs.
-->

Run both files yourself — start with a plain `python network_server.py` isn't needed; the client launches it as a subprocess automatically. Confirm the agent answers correctly for a ZIP in `known_outages` and gracefully for one that isn't.

## Modify It, Build It

<!--
  instructor: ~15 min, pairs. Good work looks like a second @mcp.tool()
  added to the server with zero changes needed on the agent side beyond
  re-running get_tools() — that's the payoff moment, make sure they notice
  they didn't have to touch agent.py's tool-wiring logic at all.
-->

Add a second tool to `network_server.py` — a billing lookup, a ticket-status check, anything a real telecom rep would need — and confirm your agent can call it after only restarting the client. You should not need to change how `agent.py` is wired up.
